paras: The killing of Griffin Ingram was the shooting of a Black man by a member of a constable's posse on the Ponchatolowa in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, on June 21, 1882. Ingram was wanted on a warrant from Livingston parish, accused of murdering his young son, and the local paper reported that he was shot while resisting arrest. An inquest was held on his body, and the parish later paid its costs.

According to the St. Tammany Farmer, Ingram was accused of killing his son, a boy of about twelve, in Livingston parish a few weeks before his death. The paper alleged that he beat the boy for taking a piece of meat without permission, broke his neck, shot him and staked the body to the ground in the woods. The Governor offered a $500 reward for his arrest, and Ingram had been "lurking" in St. Tammany Parish for some time.

On Wednesday, June 21, a constable from Livingston parish holding a warrant for Ingram came upon him with a posse while he was burning charcoal on the Ponchatolowa. By the account the paper printed, Ingram told them he would never be taken alive and resisted, and the officers were "finally led to shoot him." The fatal shot was fired by a posse member identified only as Mr. Davis. The end of the report is garbled in the surviving text, and no other version of the encounter appears in the coverage.

Proceedings of the St. Tammany police jury, meeting on October 9, 1882, list a $10 bill from Justice of the Peace Matthew Dicks for holding an inquest on the body of Griffin Ingram, dated June 21, 1882. Five men, George Callahan, Aug. Shultz, Hezekiah Strain, Alexander Davis and Thos. Corcoran, were paid $2 each as jurors at that inquest. Dicks and Constable Joe Matthews also billed small fees under "State vs. Griffin Ingram," but no verdict of the inquest is printed and no inquiry into the shooting itself was found.

The only coverage found is in the Covington weekly St. Tammany Farmer, which ran the story on June 24 under the headline "KILLED WHILE RESISTING ARREST." Most of that report described the alleged murder of the boy, calling it "a most shocking one," and it presented the officers' version of the shooting as fact. On July 15 the paper noted that the Capitolian-Advocate was still advertising the $500 reward for "the colored murderer, Griffin Ingram," and remarked, "Might as well take it out. Ingram is gone for good." The police jury proceedings naming the inquest were reprinted in the Farmer through the autumn of 1882.
No Black-press coverage exists for this period, and no other white paper's report was found.

reader.title: Killing of Griffin Ingram
bases: A constable from Livingston parish serving a warrant came upon Ingram with a posse, and one posse member, Mr. Davis, shot him dead, reported as during resistance to arrest (A1, A2).

Ingram was killed by a member of a constable's posse acting on a warrant, and the only account, from the officers' side, says he was shot while resisting arrest; nothing in the coverage describes a mob or an extralegal killing, and the posse's size is not given (A1, A3).

All reports come from one weekly, the St. Tammany Farmer, whose news account (A1) rests on the officers' version; its later notice (A2) and the police jury bills for an inquest (A3, A6) confirm the death and date but add no independent account of the shooting.
